A collection of books, essays, people, and tools exploring how computers, representations, interfaces, and learning environments can augment human thought and change what we are capable of understanding.

*(Generated by ChatGPT.)*

## Start Here

### Bret Victor

* **[Media for Thinking the Unthinkable](https://worrydream.com/MediaForThinkingTheUnthinkable/)**

  * A foundational exploration of how new computational representations can make previously difficult ideas easier to see, manipulate, and understand.

* **[The Humane Representation of Thought](https://worrydream.com/)**

  * On designing representations and interfaces that work with the way humans actually think.

* **[The Future of Programming](https://worrydream.com/dbx/)**

  * A critique of conventional programming environments and an argument for fundamentally different ways of thinking about programming.

### Douglas Engelbart

* **[Augmenting Human Intellect](https://www.dougengelbart.org/content/view/138/)** (1962)

  * One of the foundational texts for the entire tools-for-thought tradition.
  * Introduces the idea of using computers to augment human intellectual capabilities rather than simply automate existing tasks.

### Alan Kay

* **“User Interface: A Personal View”**

  * Explores the idea that computers could fundamentally change human thought and civilization.
  * Particularly important for understanding Kay's vision of computers as dynamic media.

### Vannevar Bush

* **[“As We May Think”](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1945/07/as-we-may-think/303881/)** (1945)

  * The intellectual ancestor of hypertext, personal knowledge systems, and many later visions of augmented cognition.
  * Introduces the hypothetical **Memex**.

### Andy Matuschak

* **[Andy Matuschak's Notes](https://andymatuschak.org/)**

  * A large collection of interconnected notes exploring learning, knowledge systems, software, and tools for thought.
  * Particularly relevant:

    * Evergreen notes
    * Programmable attention
    * Enabling environments
    * Tools for tools for thought
    * Why books don't work

* **“Why Books Don't Work”**

  * An argument that conventional books are poorly matched to how people actually learn and remember.

### Michael Nielsen & Andy Matuschak

* **[Quantum Country](https://quantum.country/)**

  * An experimental “mnemonic medium” designed around active recall and spaced repetition.
  * One of the clearest examples of the ideas in this reading list being turned into an actual medium for learning.

## Historical Lineage

### Vannevar Bush

**“As We May Think”**

The Memex establishes an early vision of a machine for extending human memory and navigating information associatively.

### Douglas Engelbart

**“Augmenting Human Intellect”**

Moves from storing information toward actively augmenting human problem-solving.

### Alan Kay

Treats computers as a new kind of **medium**, rather than merely calculating machines.

### Ted Nelson

* **Computer Lib / Dream Machines**
* Developed the concept of **hypertext**.
* A much more radical and unconventional vision of interconnected digital information.

### Bret Victor

Brings many of these ideas into modern interface design, interactive explanations, and computational media.

---

## Tools for Thought

### Maggie Appleton

* **[Tools for Thought as Cultural Practices, not Computational Objects](https://maggieappleton.com/tools-for-thought)**

  * A useful overview of the history and culture surrounding tools for thought.
  * Particularly useful for understanding why these tools are more than productivity software.

### Howard Rheingold

* ***Tools for Thought: The History and Future of Mind-Expanding Technology***

  * A historical account of the tools-for-thought movement.
  * Covers Engelbart, Xerox PARC, personal computing, and the development of technologies intended to extend human cognition.

## Interactive Learning & Explanations

### Explorable Explanations

A design philosophy associated especially with Bret Victor: explanations should allow the reader to manipulate the underlying ideas rather than merely read about them.

Explore:

* **Bret Victor's interactive essays**
* **Nicky Case's interactive explanations**
* **The Evolution of Trust**
* **Parable of the Polygons**

### Nicky Case

Particularly interesting for demonstrating how simulations can communicate systems and emergent behavior.

---

## Computational Notebooks

Computational notebooks are one of the clearest examples of a new medium emerging from the needs of people doing intellectual work.

### Jupyter

A computational notebook environment combining:

* prose
* code
* data
* visualizations
* experimentation
* executable results

The important idea isn't simply “code in a document.” It's the ability to **think through a problem while constructing and manipulating its representation**.

### Observable

A browser-based computational notebook environment particularly oriented toward interactive data visualization and exploration.

---

## Learning Through Environment

### Seymour Papert

Explore Papert's work on:

* Constructionism
* Logo
* Learning through making
* Computers as environments for thinking

Papert is particularly important if you're interested in the question:

> What happens when the learning environment itself becomes programmable?

### Christopher Alexander

Although not primarily about computing or education, Alexander's work on **patterns, environments, and generative systems** provides an interesting conceptual bridge to designing environments that enable particular kinds of thought and behavior.

### Donella Meadows

Explore:

* ***Thinking in Systems***
* Systems thinking
* Feedback loops
* Mental models
* Leverage points

This connects naturally to interactive simulations and computational representations of complex systems.

---

## Games as Learning Environments

### *The Witness* — Jonathan Blow

A game built around discovering rules and developing perceptual models through interaction with the environment.

Particularly interesting as an example of **learning without explicit instruction**.

### Nicky Case

Interactive games and explanations that teach systems by letting the player manipulate them.

---

## Software as a Thinking Medium

### Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (SICP)

A classic programming text that treats programming as a medium for constructing, manipulating, and understanding abstractions.

Worth approaching less as “a book about learning Lisp” and more as:

> What does programming allow us to think about that we couldn't easily think about otherwise?

---

## Memory & Retrieval

### Anki

A practical implementation of:

* Spaced repetition
* Active recall
* Incremental learning
* Memory scheduling

Interesting in the context of the broader question:

> How can software become part of the learning process rather than merely a place where information is stored?

### Quantum Country

An especially interesting combination of:

* Hypertext
* Explanatory writing
* Active recall
* Spaced repetition
* Interactive learning

### SuperMemo Guru & Piotr Wozniak

#### [SuperMemo Guru](https://supermemo.guru/wiki/)

**Piotr Wozniak** — creator of SuperMemo and pioneer of spaced repetition and incremental reading.

SuperMemo Guru is a huge body of writing about **memory, learning, creativity, problem solving, and knowledge management**. It belongs directly in the tools-for-thought lineage because Wozniak isn't merely describing better study habits; he is exploring how software can fundamentally change the way knowledge is acquired, organized, processed, and retained.

See also: [SuperMemopedia](https://supermemopedia.com/wiki/Main_Page).

#### Incremental Reading

The most important concept to explore.

Instead of:

> Read one article → finish it → move on → forget most of it.

Incremental reading treats a large body of information as a living queue. You read small portions of many sources, extract what matters, revisit those fragments later, progressively distill them, and eventually convert important ideas into questions for long-term recall.

This connects particularly well to:

* **Douglas Engelbart** — augmenting human intellect
* **Ted Nelson** — nonlinear information
* **Andy Matuschak** — knowledge systems and mnemonic media
* **Bret Victor** — new representations for thinking
* **Quantum Country** — computationally augmented learning
* **Anki** — spaced repetition and active recall

#### Read These

* **[Inevitability of Incremental Reading](https://supermemo.guru/wiki/Inevitability_of_incremental_reading)**

  * Wozniak's broader argument for why incremental reading emerges naturally from the problem of managing large amounts of knowledge.

* **[20 Rules of Knowledge Formulation](https://supermemo.guru/wiki/20_rules_of_knowledge_formulation)**

  * Principles for converting information into knowledge that can actually be remembered.

* **[History of SuperMemo](https://supermemo.guru/wiki/History_of_SuperMemo)**

  * Useful historical context for active recall, spaced repetition, SuperMemo, and incremental reading.

#### The Bigger Idea

SuperMemo is particularly interesting because it treats **memory itself as something software can augment**.

The progression is roughly:

**Bush:** augment external memory

→ **Engelbart:** augment intellectual work

→ **Nelson:** augment nonlinear information

→ **Kay:** computers as a new medium

→ **Victor:** new computational representations

→ **Matuschak:** augment learning and attention

→ **Wozniak:** augment the acquisition and retention of knowledge

That makes SuperMemo Guru one of the most relevant rabbit holes in the entire reading list.

## A Five-Item Starting Path

If the entire list is too much, start here:

1. **Bret Victor — Media for Thinking the Unthinkable**
2. **Bret Victor — The Humane Representation of Thought**
3. **Douglas Engelbart — Augmenting Human Intellect**
4. **Andy Matuschak — Notes**
5. **Quantum Country**

Then read **Howard Rheingold's *Tools for Thought*** for the historical context.

---

## Central Question

The common thread running through all of this:

> **What kinds of thinking become possible when we design the medium around the mind, rather than forcing the mind to adapt to the medium?**
